h1:
Walking Paknam Old Town
Market, Fort & Ferry on the Chao Phraya
intro: Paknam is the old town at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River, just a ride to the end of the BTS Green Line from Bangkok. Step off at Paknam station and a few minutes' walk gets you to a riverside fresh market, an old Chinese shrine, early-Rattanakosin-era forts, and a ferry crossing that locals still use every day. It's an easy half-day to full-day trip you can do entirely on foot, no car needed.

blocks.html: A lot of people know Samut Prakan by its nickname "Paknam," because the town sits right where the Chao Phraya River empties into the Gulf of Thailand. It used to be Bangkok's front gate, lined with forts to fend off enemies coming in from the sea. Today the traces of the old town still mix in with the fresh market, long-running food stalls, and a riverside life where people still ride the ferry across. We walked it ourselves, so here's what a half-day to full-day in Paknam old town actually looks like.

blocks.text: Paknam Market — the heart of the old town

blocks.html: The best place to start is Paknam Market, a fresh market on the Chao Phraya River that's been part of the town forever. It's a short walk from BTS Paknam toward the ferry pier. Inside it's a maze of seafood stalls — shrimp, shellfish, crab, fish — both fresh and dried, like salted fish, shrimp paste, and sun-dried squid. Prices run cheaper than markets in the city because it's right by the sea and the stock turns over fast. Just walking through is fun, but come in the morning for the liveliest atmosphere and the freshest catch.

The appeal of Paknam Market isn't only the seafood — it's the long-running eateries tucked away in the side lanes. Many have been going for decades, the kind of places Paknam locals have eaten at since their parents' day. Do a loop, then pick a spot or two to sit down and eat.

blocks.title: When to come
blocks.html: The fresh market is busiest from morning to late morning, when the seafood is freshest and every shop is open. By late afternoon some stalls have already sold out, so if you're set on a famous spot, come before noon.

blocks.html: These are the spots Paknam locals bring up the most that are still open. Most are within walking distance of each other around the market, and prices in this area are easy on the wallet.

items.name: Paknam Fresh Fish Noodles
items.blurb: A long-established fish noodle shop with big chunks of fish and a sweet, fishy broth that isn't muddy. It's the day-opener the neighborhood knows well.

items.name: Jay Juk Yentafo
items.blurb: A famous yentafo spot that nearly every Paknam local recommends. Known for the hot-pot yentafo and crispy fried wontons, bold and local in flavor.

items.name: Hoi Tod To Rung (old recipe)
items.blurb: Oyster omelette made the old way with duck egg as its signature, crisp outside and soft inside. Open late, perfect for a dinner stop after walking the market.

items.name: Jai Dee Shaved Ice
items.blurb: An old-school shaved ice shop that's part of Paknam Market. Plenty of toppings to choose from, big bowls, light prices — a sweet finish after walking in the sun.

items.name: Amnuay Phanit Sticky Rice
items.blurb: An old-school sweet sticky rice that Paknam locals buy as a snack or a gift to bring home. Eat it with custard or other toppings — just the right balance of sweet and rich.

items.name: Paknam Old-Recipe Red Pork Rice
items.blurb: Red pork and crispy pork over rice with an old-recipe sauce. Quick and filling, friendly on the wallet — an easy lunch between sightseeing.

blocks.html: If that's not enough, the lanes inside the market have plenty more small shops — pork satay, dumplings, peanut brittle, and seasonal snacks. You can graze your way through at an easy pace.

blocks.text: The City Pillar Shrine — Paknam's enduring faith

blocks.html: Not far from the market is the Samut Prakan City Pillar Shrine on Prakhon Chai Road. It started as a Thai-style shrine and was later rebuilt as a red-and-gold Chinese-style temple, long held in reverence by Paknam locals. Inside there's an open courtyard and some nice photo corners. It's open roughly 8:30–16:30. If you like paying respects or photographing Chinese architecture, drop by before or after walking the market.

blocks.text: Phlaeng Faifa Fort — traces of a frontier town

blocks.html: In the early Rattanakosin era, Samut Prakan was set up as a defensive line against enemies coming by sea, so several forts were built along the river mouth. Phlaeng Faifa Fort is one of the old forts that still has traces left to see. It's a good stop for anyone interested in history, and it helps you understand why the town is called "Paknam" (river mouth) and just how important it once was as Bangkok's gateway to the sea.

items: The historical angle — the forts around Paknam were built to guard against attacks by boat. Seen together with Phra Samut Chedi, the riverside line of defense becomes much clearer.
Who it's for — people who like old towns, history, and photographing old architecture, more than those looking for flashy attractions.
Check before you go — some old fort sites are government or military land, so check the opening days and hours in advance, as they may not be open every day.

blocks.text: Take the ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi

blocks.html: The highlight you shouldn't skip is heading down to Wibun Si Pier in Paknam Market and taking the ferry across to the other bank to reach Phra Samut Chedi, the old white pagoda that once stood in the middle of the river back in the reign of Rama II (the land has since silted up and joined the bank). On the crossing you get wide views of the Chao Phraya River, cargo boats, and the riverside life on both sides — a short ride that's genuinely lovely.

items: Fare — adjusted to 8 THB per trip for the general public (from 1 April 2026); 4 THB for students and uniformed civil servants.
Ferry hours — service starts in the early morning around 04:30 and runs until about 21:30, with frequent departures so you won't wait long.
Once across — it's only a few hundred meters' walk from the pier on the chedi side to Phra Samut Chedi itself, with small food and souvenir shops along the way.

blocks.title: Ferry tips
blocks.html: Have coins or small notes ready for the fare to make things easier, and if you want good photos, stand by the railing on the side facing out over the river. In the late afternoon the soft light makes the view especially nice.

blocks.text: Walking Paknam old town with no car

blocks.html: Paknam is most fun on foot, since the highlights cluster around the market and the ferry pier. Here's a half-day to full-day plan you can run straight from BTS Paknam.

items.activity: Get off at BTS Paknam, walk into Paknam Market, and check out the seafood and dried-goods stalls.
items.note: Freshest catch and full shops in the morning

items.activity: Have breakfast at an old-school spot, like the fresh fish noodles or Jay Juk yentafo.
items.note: Some famous shops sell out before afternoon

items.activity: Walk to Wibun Si Pier and take the ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi.
items.note: Fare is 8 THB, ferries run often

items.activity: Walk up to Phra Samut Chedi, pay your respects, take photos, then catch the ferry back.
items.note: Small souvenir shops on the chedi side

blocks.label: Full day
blocks.title: Add the afternoon & evening (on top of the half day)

items.activity: Head back to the Paknam side and stop at the City Pillar Shrine to pay respects and photograph the Chinese shrine.
Drop by Phlaeng Faifa Fort and the old-town traces, for those who like history.
Walk the evening market, try the shaved ice at Jai Dee, and pick up dried goods to take home.
items.note: Paknam dried goods are well priced

items.activity: Finish with dinner at Hoi Tod To Rung or a riverside spot, and soak up the evening atmosphere.

blocks.text: Getting there and things to know

items: BTS — take the Green Line to Paknam station (the southern end of the line), then walk or hop on a motorbike taxi into the market in a few minutes. Easy, and no parking to hunt for.
By car — you can drive, but parking around the market gets tight on weekends. Better to park near the mall by the station and walk in.
What to wear — lots of walking and strong sun by the river, so wear comfortable shoes, bring an umbrella or hat, and carry water.
Cash — most market shops and the ferry fare take cash, so have small notes and coins ready.

faq.q: How long does it take to walk Paknam old town?
faq.a: A half day covers the main spots — walking Paknam Market, eating at the old-school shops, and taking the ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi. If you also want to stop at the City Pillar Shrine and the old fort, make it an easy full-day trip.

faq.q: How much is the Paknam ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi?
faq.a: The general-public fare was adjusted to 8 THB per trip from 1 April 2026 (previously 6 THB); students and uniformed civil servants pay 4 THB. The ferry leaves from Wibun Si Pier in Paknam Market.

faq.q: What time does the Paknam ferry run?
faq.a: The ferry starts service in the early morning around 04:30 and runs until about 21:30, with frequent departures so you won't wait long — good for both early visitors and evening trips.

faq.q: Can I get to Paknam by BTS?
faq.a: Yes. Take the Green Line to Paknam station, which is the southern terminus, then walk or take a motorbike taxi into Paknam Market and the pier in a few minutes — no need to drive yourself.

faq.q: What's good to eat at Paknam Market?
faq.a: It's known for fresh, well-priced seafood and long-running eateries like the fresh fish noodles, Jay Juk yentafo, Hoi Tod To Rung, Jai Dee shaved ice, and Amnuay Phanit sticky rice. You can graze across several spots in one area.
